Newton's 3 Laws of Motion 🚀

Newton's Laws of Motion explain why objects move, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction.

They were developed by Isaac Newton and are the foundation of classical physics.

We'll learn each law with simple explanations, real-life examples, and a quick quiz at the end!

1. Newton's First Law — The Law of Inertia

An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at a constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force.

In simpler words:

A soccer ball won't move until you kick it.

A moving ball will keep moving unless something slows it down or changes its direction.

Friction and air resistance are forces that can slow things down.

Real-life example: When a car suddenly stops, your body tends to keep moving forward. That's why seatbelts are important!

Remember

Inertia means an object's resistance to changes in its velocity. More mass means more inertia.
2. Newton's Second Law — Force = Mass × Acceleration

This law explains how forces change an object's motion.

nzherald.co.nz
F = ma

Net Force = Mass × Acceleration

Here's what the letters mean:

F = Net force, measured in newtons (N)

m = Mass, measured in kilograms (kg)

a = Acceleration, measured in m/s²

Example: Imagine pushing an empty shopping cart versus a full one. The full cart requires more force to accelerate at the same rate because it has more mass.

Try changing the force and mass

Mass

5 kg

Net force

20 N

Resulting acceleration

4.00 m/s²

20 ÷ 5 = 4.00

Try increasing the mass while keeping the force the same. What happens to acceleration?

Key idea: More net force means more acceleration. More mass means less acceleration for the same net force.

3. Newton's Third Law — Action and Reaction

For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

launchphotography.com

Imagine a rocket launching into space.

The rocket pushes exhaust gases downward.

The gases push the rocket upward with an equal and opposite force.

This helps the rocket accelerate upward.

Another example is jumping. Your feet push the ground downward, and the ground pushes you upward.

Important: The two forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel each other out on one object.

The easiest way to remember Newton's laws is:

1st Law: Objects resist changes in motion.

2nd Law: Forces cause acceleration.

3rd Law: Forces always come in pairs.

Once you understand these three ideas, you can explain everything from kicking a soccer ball to launching a spacecraft!

states.text:
Yes! Newton's three laws of motion apply in space too! 🚀 In fact, space is one of the best places to understand them because there's very little air resistance or friction.

1. First Law — Inertia in Space

Imagine an astronaut floating in space who throws a ball.

The ball keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed if no net force acts on it.

Unlike on Earth, there's almost no air resistance to slow it down.

However, gravity from nearby planets, stars, and other objects can change its motion.

Fun fact: A spacecraft can coast through space without continuously firing its engines!

2. Second Law — F = ma in Space
space.com

Suppose an astronaut pushes a 10 kg object with a net force of 20 N.

Using Newton's second law:

The object accelerates at 2 m/s², just as it would on Earth under the same net force.

3. Third Law — Rockets Work in Space
spacevoyageventures.com

A common misconception is that rockets need air to push against.

They don't!

The rocket pushes exhaust gases backward.

The exhaust gases push the rocket forward.

This works even in the vacuum of space!

That's Newton's third law.

But there's one important detail!

Newton's laws are extremely accurate for ordinary spacecraft motion, but they have limitations.

At speeds close to the speed of light, we need Einstein's special relativity. For extremely strong gravity or very precise calculations, we may need general relativity.

Quick question for you 🧠

If an astronaut throws a ball in deep space, far from significant gravitational influences, what will happen to it?

A. It will gradually slow down and stop.
B. It will continue moving at constant velocity.
C. It will accelerate forever.

Exactly! 🎯 You've understood Newton's First Law!

An object in motion will keep moving forever at the same speed and in the same direction, as long as no net external force acts on it.

This happens because of inertia.

🚀 Imagine this experiment in space

You're an astronaut floating in deep space, far away from planets and stars.

You throw a ball at 10 m/s.

Assuming no external forces act on it:

Time after throwing

	

Speed




1 second

	

10 m/s




1 minute

	

10 m/s




1 hour

	

10 m/s




1 year

	

10 m/s




1 million years

	

10 m/s

The ball would continue moving at 10 m/s indefinitely!

But why do objects stop on Earth?

Imagine rolling a ball across the floor.

It eventually stops because of:

Friction between the ball and the floor.

Air resistance opposing its motion.

Without these forces (or any other net force), the ball would continue moving.

Here's something interesting! 🧠

Inertia doesn't actually push an object forward.

An object doesn't need a force to keep moving. It only needs a net force to change its velocity.

That's one of Newton's most important discoveries.

Let me challenge you with a question!

If a spaceship is traveling through deep space at 20,000 km/h and suddenly turns off its engines, what happens?

A. It immediately stops.
B. It gradually slows down.
C. It keeps moving at 20,000 km/h.
